{{Short description|Special circle in geometry}}
[[File:Taylor-Kreis.svg|thumb|upright=1.37|The feet of the perpendiculars <math>P_{ab},P_{ac},P_{ba}, P_{bc},P_{ca},P_{cb} </math> lie on a common circle]]
The '''Taylor circle''' is a special [[circle]] associated with a [[triangle]]. It is named after [[Henry Martyn Taylor]] (1842–1927), who discussed it in 1882.<ref>Claudi Alsina, Roger B. Nelsen: ''Icons of Mathematics. An Exploration of Twenty Key Images''. Springer, 2011, {{ISBN|978-0-88385-986-5}}, pp. 112–113 ({{Google books|jl_0DwAAQBAJ|excerpt (Google)|page=112}})</ref> However it was already considered by [[Eugène Charles Catalan]] in 1879 and first proposed by the French mathematician [[Eutaris]] in 1877.<ref>[https://www.cut-the-knot.org/triangle/Taylor.shtml Taylor-Kreis] at cut-the-knot.org (retrieved 2024-0-2-9)</ref>

Consider the three feet of the three [[Altitude (triangle)|altitudes of triangle]]. For each foot of an altitude construct the [[perpendicular]]s onto the two other triangles sides. The intersections of those perpendiculars with the triangles sides yield six points and those six points are located on a common circle, the Taylor circle.<ref>Roger A. Johnson: ''Advanced Euclidean Geometry''. Dover 2007, {{ISBN|978-0-486-46237-0}}, p. 277</ref>

The radius of the Taylor circle can be computed by the following formula taking the three angles of a triangle and the radius of its [[circumcircle]]:<ref>{{MathWorld|TaylorCircle|Taylor Circle}}</ref>

: <math>r_T = R\sqrt{\sin^2\alpha\sin^2\beta\sin^2\gamma+\cos^2\alpha\cos^2\beta\cos^2\gamma}</math>
